newsitem.title: UK: ICCO to set up reserve fund from cocoa buffer stock.
newsitem.headline: ICCO to set up reserve fund from cocoa buffer stock.

text.p: Cocoa producers and consumers agreed to set up a reserve fund of three million stg from buffer stock revenues for the eventual liquidation of the International Cocoa Organization (ICCO), delegates said on Monday.

The ICCO Council adopted the decision by consensus on Friday after week-long negotiations continued into the night in attempts to break an impasse that some delegates said was beginning to threaten the structure of the organization.
Brazil remained opposed to the decision. It had been campaigning for a decoupling of the reserve fund from buffer stock revenues, to which it was the biggest contributor in the 1970s.
It was also against using the interest generated on the fund to plug the ICCO's budget shortfalls when buffer stock sales end in March 1998.
But Tim Mordan, the UK representative and chairman of the ICCO executive committee, said the decision was binding on all members.
An ICCO spokeswoman said an initial 1.5 stg would be set aside from the buffer stock proceeds and put into an interest bearing account on April 1.
However the formula for the remaining 1.5 million stg was yet to be decided.

The council's decision read: "The modalities of apportionment between exporting and importing members of the second half of this amount (three million stg) shall be decided upon by the council after due consideration of all relevant legal and administrative aspects".
Delegates said the ICCO was left explore different options for the the second half of the fund, including asking member countries that did not participate in the buffer stocks to contribute.
The financing of the reserve fund was a stumbling block in last week's ICCO talks after a decision was delayed in December's meeting.
Producers, who funded 80 percent of the buffer stock money, were initially opposed to deducting any money from that account and instead favoured a spike in members' contributions.
Consumers meanwhile were reluctant to seek separate funding. They were keen to create the fund at once and channel the interest income to administration of the ICCO.
The decision on the remaining 1.5 million stg may feature more of such disagreements in the next ICCO meeting in June.

"We are reasonably happy. Ideally we would have preferred to have three million taken out from the buffer stock and start earning interest on that straight away but producers had problems with that," Mordan said.
The ICCO has still 51,000 tonnes of cocoa to liquidate, out of a total 250,000 tonnes it started selling in 1993 after the system proved ineffective as a mechanism to lift low prices.
The last 1.5 tranches of the buffer stock revenues, expected to total around $300 million, will be distributed in September and next March.
